title: Across the Trojan Plain
author: Robert Thornett
summary: Robert Thornett, a Humane Letters teacher at Chandler Prep, takes up Strabo's claim that Homer, not Eratosthenes, was the true father of geography because his poetry teaches why landscapes matter to human choices. Using the Trojan Plain as his case, Thornett argues the plain is not a backdrop to the Iliad but a force that creates visibility, mobility, and vulnerability. Its open sightlines make kleos, a public form of glory, possible while exposing leaders to scrutiny, which is why Sarpedon insists Lycian nobles must earn their honors by fighting in front. The flat expanse also enables the momentum of aristeiai like Ajax's river-like charge, yet Zeus can halt Diomedes with a lightning bolt, imposing a boundary where nature provides none. Thornett shows how the same openness punishes retreat, as Hector ignores Polydamas's warning, and exposes the naive spy Dolon to veterans who read the terrain better. The climax is Achilles's hubristic assault on the river Scamander, a transgression of both physical and cosmic boundaries answered by the landscape itself. The piece models Great Books close reading as a way to teach how place shapes action and the limits of human ambition.
points: Following Strabo, Thornett treats Homeric geography as 'primitive philosophy' that explains why places shape human choices rather than merely recording them.
The Trojan Plain's unobstructed views make public glory (kleos) possible but also leave kings and heroes nowhere to hide from scrutiny, even from a commoner like Thersites.
Sarpedon's speech to Glaucus frames leadership as a duty to be visibly at the front, earning inherited aristocratic status through exposure to danger.
Hector's dismissal of Polydamas shows a failure to see that the open terrain enabling his advance would make a later retreat catastrophic.
Achilles's attack on the Scamander River illustrates hubris as transgression against physis, the natural order, which answers with overwhelming latent power.
quotes: While Eratosthenes criticizes Homer for prioritizing amusement over instruction—myths and monsters over hard data—Strabo responds that Homer’s myths and poetry were in fact instruction, in something more profound than basic facts: a “primitive philosophy.” Geography is philosophic because it asks why landscapes matter. Time and again, Homer illustrates how the places he describes influence human choices. The role of the Trojan Plain in The Iliad is a prime example.

The plain is not just the setting for The Iliad. It creates the visibility, mobility, and vulnerability that influence how warriors maneuver and earn glory. In some ways, the flat plain is egalitarian, while in others it reinforces rigid class structures.

But the openness of the plain exposes the success and failure of both heroes and common soldiers alike. Its unbroken views erase privacy and leave nowhere to hide: no forests to disappear into, no ridges to mask movement, no caves to regroup inside.

These Lycian and Cretan commanders both recognize that leadership does not bestow a license to hide, but rather a responsibility to visibly represent the community in the heart of the fray. Sarpedon recognizes that the very danger of being the exposed battlefield on the plain presents an opportunity to show courage, and thus to demonstrate that his aristocratic status is not just inherited, but earned.

In an unobstructed space devoid of natural boundaries, Zeus imposes his own. His ability to produce an impassable barrier amid emptiness illustrates that even the ground heroes stand on is subject to divine power.

Hector correctly credits Zeus for the Trojans’ success thus far, but he fails to recognize that later, in retreat, the same open terrain that facilitated his advance could bring defeat, as eventually it does.

Here, Achilles shows a lack of sophrosyne (moderation, restraint) as he transgresses two sorts of boundaries: the physical river that guards Troy and, in the act of polluting and attacking it, the cosmological boundary between humanity and divinity. As the literal embodiment of the landscape, Scamander rises to halt the hubris-driven fury of the greatest mortal warrior.

In The Iliad, Homer shows how the Trojan Plain is far more than a backdrop to the war. Its openness creates possibilities that shape battle strategies, paths to glory, and the limits of human ambition. Time and again, characters who understand the possibilities the landscape presents are able to exploit them, while those who do not, suffer the consequences.
